title: The Five Suns
source_ref: Leyenda de los Soles (Codex Chimalpopoca, 1558) and the Florentine Codex, Book 7
paragraphs: Before this world there were four others, each named for a day in the 260-day calendar. The Leyenda de los Soles tells of Four Jaguar, whose people were devoured by jaguars; Four Wind, which ended in a great wind and turned survivors into monkeys; Four Rain, destroyed by a rain of fire; and Four Water, a flood that turned people into fish.

The names and order of the first four suns, the gods who rule them and the length of each age vary between colonial texts. The Leyenda de los Soles, a Nahuatl account copied in 1558, keeps Four Jaguar, Four Wind, Four Rain and Four Water. The Florentine Codex and the earlier Historia de los Mexicanos por sus Pinturas give their own versions and assign different gods to the same age.

When the fourth sun drowned, the gods gathered in the dark at Teotihuacan, a city already ancient and empty. Its later Nahua name means 'place where the gods were made.' Two gods volunteered to throw themselves into a great fire: Nanahuatzin, poor and covered in sores, and Tecuciztecatl, rich and proud. Tecuciztecatl hesitated; Nanahuatzin leapt in and became the sun.

Tecuciztecatl followed and became the moon, dimmed by a rabbit thrown into his face. The sun hung still until the gods sacrificed themselves, and Ehecatl, the wind, blew it into motion. So began the fifth sun, Four Movement, which will end in earthquake. The Mexica later saw their patron Huitzilopochtli in the rising sun, and fed it with offerings.
notes: The Leyenda de los Soles survives in the Codex Chimalpopoca, a Nahuatl manuscript copied in 1558. The Florentine Codex and the Historia de los Mexicanos por sus Pinturas give different lists of the first four suns and different ruling gods. The rabbit in the moon, the number of years in each age and the identity of the fifth sun's god (Nanahuatzin, Tonatiuh or Huitzilopochtli) vary by source. The story is a colonial-era record of older oral and painted traditions.

title: Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca Make the Earth
source_ref: Leyenda de los Soles (Codex Chimalpopoca, 1558), with later Nahua accounts
paragraphs: After the fourth sun drowned, the gods looked for a place to stand. They saw Cipactli, the earth monster, swimming in the primeval water: a crocodile-like body covered with mouths at every joint, always hungry. The Leyenda de los Soles calls her Tlaltecuhtli, and the two names are often used for the same being. Nothing could rest on the water while she devoured it.

Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca turned themselves into two serpents. One seized her left hand and the other her right foot, and they pulled until her body tore in two. From one half they made the sky, from the other the earth. In some versions Tezcatlipoca loses a foot in the struggle, which is why he limps.

Her body became the world's food and features. Her hair turned into trees, flowers and herbs; her skin into grass; her eyes into springs and wells; her mouth into rivers and caves; her nose into valleys; her shoulders into mountains. The gods decreed that the earth would give forth plants, and that people would live on what grew from her.

But the torn goddess did not become a passive landscape. The sources say she sometimes cried out at night, asking for blood and hearts, and the gods granted her offerings so the earth would keep producing. This is a cosmological explanation for sacrifice, not a celebration of killing. It imagines the ground as a living body that must be fed.
notes: The Leyenda de los Soles names the torn earth being Tlaltecuhtli, while other colonial accounts and modern retellings call her Cipactli; the two are often merged. The assignment of body parts, the loss of Tezcatlipoca's foot, and whether other gods helped vary. The detail that the earth demands blood is an etiological explanation for sacrifice, not evidence that the myth was a script for killing.

title: Coatlicue and the Birth of Huitzilopochtli
source_ref: Florentine Codex, Book 3, and the Coyolxauhqui stone from the Templo Mayor
paragraphs: Coatlicue, whose name means Serpent Skirt, was a mother goddess and priestess. She swept the shrine on Coatepec, Serpent Mountain, and lived with her daughter Coyolxauhqui and her four hundred sons, the Centzon Huitznahua. One day a ball of feathers fell from the sky. She gathered it and placed it at her breast, and it made her pregnant. Her children were furious at the shame they believed she had brought.

Coyolxauhqui led the four hundred against their mother. One of the brothers, Cuahuitlicac, warned the child in Coatlicue's womb. As the attackers reached the summit, Huitzilopochtli was born fully grown and fully armed, with a shield, darts and the xiuhcoatl, the fire serpent. He sprang up and drove them back.

He killed Coyolxauhqui, cut off her head and threw it into the sky, where it became the moon. The four hundred brothers became the stars of the south. The Florentine Codex records the story, and the great Coyolxauhqui stone found at the Templo Mayor in 1978 shows her dismembered body at the foot of the stairway, where sacrificed captives were rolled down.

The myth works on several levels at once. Cosmically, the birth of the sun at dawn defeats the moon and the stars, who return each night. Politically, Huitzilopochtli was the patron of the Mexica, the god who led them to Tenochtitlan, and his armed birth justified their wars. It is also a story about a mother, a daughter and a threatened family, and the sources do not reduce it to simple gore.
notes: The Florentine Codex is the fullest narrative, but the number of brothers (four hundred is a schematic figure for 'many'), the name of the brother who warns Huitzilopochtli, and Coyolxauhqui's fate vary. Some versions throw her head into a canyon rather than the sky. The Coyolxauhqui stone dates to the late fifteenth century, centuries after the myth, and its placement at the Templo Mayor linked the story to state ritual.

title: Quetzalcoatl in Mictlan
paragraphs: After the fourth sun drowned, the people of that age became fish, and the gods needed new people to live in the fifth world. Quetzalcoatl went down to Mictlan, the cold land of the dead, to ask its lord Mictlantecuhtli and his consort Mictecacihuatl for the bones of the old humanity. His twin Xolotl, the dog-headed evening star, went with him as guide.

Mictlantecuhtli set a test: blow a conch shell that had no holes. Quetzalcoatl called worms to bore holes through it and bees to crawl inside, and when he blew, the shell sounded across the underworld. The lord agreed to give up the bones, but he set a trap. Quetzalcoatl fell into a pit, and the bones broke and scattered.

He gathered them and carried them up to Tamoanchan, the place of origins. There the goddess Cihuacoatl ground the bones in a jade bowl, and Quetzalcoatl and the other gods let their blood fall into the mixture. From that paste the people of the fifth sun were made. Because the bones were broken, people are said to come in different sizes and shapes.

The Leyenda de los Soles is a Nahuatl text copied in 1558, and its details vary: some versions have Quetzalcoatl bleed himself, others have all the gods contribute. The Leyenda sends Xolotl with him, while the Florentine Codex tells how Xolotl refused to die and hid, becoming the axolotl. The story also explains why a dog was buried with the dead, to guide the soul across the river.
notes: The Leyenda de los Soles is the main narrative, copied in 1558, and it is not a single fixed text: the helpers, the number of trials, the role of Xolotl and the bloodletting vary. The descent has been compared with other Mesoamerican underworld journeys, and the broken bones are an etiological explanation for human difference, not a historical claim.

title: The Founding of Tenochtitlan
source_ref: Cronica Mexicayotl (c. 1598), Duran's History of the Indies of New Spain (c. 1581) and the Florentine Codex
paragraphs: The Mexica were one of the Nahua peoples who moved through central Mexico after the fall of Tula. Their own histories say they came from Aztlan, a homeland in the north, and that the god Huitzilopochtli led them. They passed through Chicomoztoc, the seven caves, and carried the god's image with them. The migration is dated traditionally to the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and the accounts were written down long afterward.

Huitzilopochtli told them to settle where they found an eagle perched on a nopal cactus. They reached the Basin of Mexico, where the older cities and the great lake lay, and were pushed onto poor land by the peoples already there. On an island in Lake Texcoco they saw the sign. There they founded Tenochtitlan, 'the place of the prickly pear cactus on the rock,' in 1325, though some sources give 1345.

The city grew through chinampas, raised fields built in the shallow water, and through canals and causeways that linked the island to the shore. At its center stood the Templo Mayor, with twin shrines to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc. The founding story gave the Mexica a sacred center and a divine mandate, and later kings used it to justify rule over other peoples.

But the founding story is not the same as the empire. For decades the Mexica were tributaries of stronger neighbors, and only after 1428, when Tenochtitlan allied with Texcoco and Tlacopan and defeated Azcapotzalco, did they become an imperial power. The Cronica Mexicayotl, Duran and the Florentine Codex tell the migration with different emphases, and the eagle-and-cactus emblem was later taken up as Mexico's national symbol.
notes: The migration and founding are known from sixteenth-century Nahuatl and Spanish accounts, including the Cronica Mexicayotl, Duran and the Florentine Codex, which differ on dates, routes and the meaning of the sign. The traditional date 1325 is debated; some sources give 1345. The eagle-and-cactus image became Mexico's national emblem in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and the serpent in the eagle's beak is a later, variable element.

title: Tlaloc and the Rain
source_ref: Florentine Codex, Books 1 and 2, with archaeology from the Templo Mayor and Teotihuacan
paragraphs: Tlaloc is the god of rain, thunder and the waters that make maize grow. He is shown with goggle eyes and fangs, and he lives in the mountains. His helpers, the tlaloque, carry great jars of water and pour them out over the fields. Thunder is the sound of those jars breaking, and the mountains are said to be hollow with water.

Rain was not automatic. At the start of the rainy season people fasted, made offerings and held ceremonies to ask Tlaloc for water, and the Florentine Codex describes the festivals and the kinds of gifts he received. The Templo Mayor gave him one of its two great shrines, beside Huitzilopochtli, and offerings of stone jars and marine shells have been found there. Maize, beans and squash depended on this cycle.

Tlalocan, his paradise, is a green and abundant place where those who die by drowning, lightning or certain water illnesses go. It is a blessed afterlife, not a hell. A famous mural at Teotihuacan, at the compound called Tepantitla, is often read as Tlalocan: it shows plants, butterflies, water and small human figures at play.

Chicomecoatl, 'Seven Serpent,' is the goddess of maize and the harvest. She belongs to the same agricultural world as Tlaloc: he sends the rain, she brings the grain. Her festivals followed the maize cycle, and she is shown with maize ears and water. This material is not one connected plot but a set of cult stories; the details come from colonial texts and archaeology, and Nahua communities still honor the rains and the maize today.
notes: This is a description of a cult and its stories rather than one narrative. The Tlalocan mural at Teotihuacan is interpreted, not labelled; the names and number of the tlaloque vary; and Chicomecoatl overlaps with other maize deities such as Xilonen and Cinteotl. The sources are colonial and archaeological, and living Nahua communities maintain their own rain and maize traditions.
